title: Crown-of-Thorns Starfish Eats Reefs. #1: It Might Be Helping Them
description: It has up to 21 arms, hundreds of toxin-tipped thorns, and it eats coral with its stomach pushed outside its body. Outbreaks can kill up to 90% of the coral on a reef. But a new Great Barrier Reef study just found something nobody expected. Here are 5 secrets of the crown-of-thorns starfish, counted down to the twist. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: This starfish actually eats coral reefs alive. And it does it with its stomach outside its body.

scenes.label: Up to 21 arms
scenes.say: It's called the crown-of-thorns starfish. Up to twenty-one arms, and covered in hundreds of toxin-tipped thorns.

scenes.label: Reef enemy #1?
scenes.say: On the Great Barrier Reef, it's treated like public enemy number one. Teams of divers hunt it, reef by reef.

scenes.label: The twist
scenes.say: But okay, here's the thing. A brand new study just found something nobody expected. And we're saving that twist for the very end.

scenes.label: ~2,000 species
scenes.say: There are roughly two thousand kinds of starfish in the ocean. Most have five arms and just sit there looking cute.
This one is different. So today we're counting down five secrets of the crown-of-thorns, from creepy to the one that flips everything.
Quick question first. Do you think this starfish is a villain or a hero? Lock in your answer. We'll see if you change it.

scenes.label: Thorny star
scenes.say: Number five. The thorns. Its scientific name, Acanthaster, roughly means thorny star. And that's a pretty honest name.

scenes.label: Spines up to 4 cm
scenes.say: Its back is packed with hundreds of spines, each up to about four centimeters long. That's longer than a paperclip.

scenes.label: Toxin-tipped
scenes.say: And these aren't just pointy. Scientists say each thorn is tipped with toxins, and the spines actually leak defence proteins.

scenes.label: Don't touch
scenes.say: If a diver gets pricked, it can cause nausea, numbness, vomiting and aching joints. So yeah, this is a look, don't touch animal.

scenes.label: Up to 80 cm
scenes.say: Now picture the size. Scientists say it can grow up to about eighty centimeters across. That's wider than a car tire.
So a giant, spiky star covered in toxins. Surely nothing in the ocean would dare to eat that, right?

scenes.label: Giant triton
scenes.say: Wrong. Meet the giant triton, a huge sea snail. It eats this starfish like the thorns don't even exist.

scenes.label: Hunts by smell
scenes.say: Researchers say the triton seems unaffected by the spines and the toxic coating. It finds its prey using scent alone.

scenes.label: Other hunters
scenes.say: And scientists used to think the triton was almost the only predator. Now we know many fish and crabs eat them too, especially young ones.

scenes.label: Stomach outside
scenes.say: Number four. How it eats. And honestly, this is the part that makes people go, wait, what?

scenes.label: Coral = animals
scenes.say: First, remember that coral isn't a rock or a plant. It's made of tiny animals called polyps, living together in a colony.

scenes.label: Stomach out
scenes.say: The starfish climbs on top of the coral. Then it pushes its own stomach out through its mouth.

scenes.label: As big as itself
scenes.say: That stomach spreads over an area nearly as big as the starfish itself. Like a wet blanket thrown over the coral.
Then it digests the living coral right there, outside its body. When it's done, it pulls the stomach back in and walks away.

scenes.label: White scar
scenes.say: What it leaves behind is a bright white patch. Just the bare coral skeleton, with the living part gone.

scenes.label: Favorite food
scenes.say: And it's picky. It prefers fast-growing corals, like branching Acropora and the big flat plate corals.

scenes.label: Up to 10 m² a year
scenes.say: One adult can eat up to ten square meters of coral every year. That's about the floor of a small bedroom.

scenes.label: 30 cm a minute
scenes.say: And it's not slow for a starfish. It walks about thirty centimeters a minute, on tiny water-powered tube feet underneath.
Okay, so one starfish eating one bedroom of coral a year. That sounds bad, but not terrible. Hold that thought.

scenes.label: Eyes on its arms
scenes.say: Number three. This starfish can see you. And it doesn't have eyes on its face. It doesn't even have a face.

scenes.label: One eye per arm
scenes.say: Scientists in Denmark and Australia found it has one little eye at the tip of each arm. So a dozen or more eyes, pointing every direction.

scenes.label: Surround vision
scenes.say: Researchers call it surround vision. It's blurry, nothing like ours, but it can spot big shapes, like a coral reef, against open blue water.

scenes.label: Sees danger
scenes.say: And here's the cool part. It can even spot slow movers, like its enemy, the giant triton, sneaking up on it.

scenes.label: Smell = panic
scenes.say: But it doesn't even need to see the snail. Australian scientists found the starfish can smell it. And when they do, they panic.

scenes.label: Starfish stampede
scenes.say: Just water that a triton has sat in is enough to scatter a whole group. They move fast and agitated. Basically a starfish stampede.

scenes.label: Scent as a shield?
scenes.say: Scientists are now exploring if that scary smell could be used to push starfish away from the most precious reefs.
So far it eats coral with its stomach, sees with its arms, and flees from a smell. But we haven't reached the scary part yet.

scenes.label: 200 million eggs
scenes.say: Number two. The hidden army. One big female can release over two hundred million eggs in a single year.
Two hundred million. That's more than the number of people living in most countries on Earth. From one starfish.

scenes.label: 10 to 30 days
scenes.say: The babies drift through the ocean as tiny plankton for about ten to thirty days. Most get eaten. But when lots survive, things get wild.

scenes.label: Baby diet: algae
scenes.say: The ones that land on the reef don't eat coral at first. They eat a pink, crusty algae instead, like little vegetarians.

scenes.label: 6.5 years waiting
scenes.say: And here's the creepy twist. In a lab experiment, babies stayed on that algae diet for six and a half years. And they were fine.

scenes.label: Peter Pan effect
scenes.say: Scientists called it the Peter Pan effect. The babies just refuse to grow up, hiding in the reef, waiting.

scenes.label: Hidden army
scenes.say: The lead researcher called them a hidden army, waiting to eat the reef as soon as the coral grows back.

scenes.label: Grown in 2 years
scenes.say: And these starfish grow up fast. One can be ready to make its own eggs by about two years old.

scenes.label: Up to 90% coral lost
scenes.say: That's how you get an outbreak. Huge numbers of starfish, all at once. Outbreaks can kill up to ninety percent of the coral on a reef.

scenes.label: Every ~15 years
scenes.say: Since the 1960s, the Great Barrier Reef has had four major outbreaks, roughly one every fifteen years.

scenes.label: 17,528 hours
scenes.say: So Australia fights back with divers. In just one year, they spent over seventeen thousand five hundred hours underwater hunting starfish.

scenes.label: 64,879 removed
scenes.say: They removed nearly sixty-five thousand starfish across two hundred twenty reefs. One by one, with a shot of vinegar or bile salts.

scenes.label: +44% coral
scenes.say: And it works. Where control is fast and steady, the reef foundation says coral cover rose by forty-four percent.
So the answer seems simple, right? Get rid of every last one. Well, that's exactly what number one is about.

scenes.label: Villain or helper?
scenes.say: Number one. The twist. A study published this fall says this reef killer might actually be helping the reef.

scenes.label: One Tree Reef
scenes.say: Scientists from the University of Sydney watched starfish at One Tree Reef, a protected spot on the Great Barrier Reef.

scenes.label: No outbreak
scenes.say: This reef is a marine reserve. It has lots of healthy fish, and those fish keep starfish numbers low. So no outbreak. Just a normal amount.

scenes.label: Bite scars
scenes.say: From 2022 to 2024, the team tracked the white feeding scars, one by one, to see what really happens after a starfish eats.

scenes.label: ~75% survived
scenes.say: And here's the surprise. After almost seventy-five percent of the feeding events, the coral was still alive.

scenes.label: 188 of 260
scenes.say: In one survey month, a hundred eighty-eight out of two hundred sixty bitten colonies still had living tissue. The starfish took a bite and moved on.

scenes.label: Slow corals regrow
scenes.say: Some of the scars even started to heal. Slow-growing corals, like Porites and Montipora, grew back over the white patches.

scenes.label: Fast corals cut back
scenes.say: But the fast-growing Acropora corals, the starfish's favorite, didn't regrow. And that's actually the key.

scenes.label: Space for others
scenes.say: Scientists think fast corals can crowd a reef, like weeds in a garden. By trimming them, a few starfish make space for slower corals to survive.

scenes.label: More variety
scenes.say: Scientists say a little bit of damage, not too much, can actually keep a reef more varied. More kinds of coral, not fewer.

scenes.label: Not eliminate
scenes.say: The lead scientist said once an outbreak is stopped, the goal should not necessarily be to wipe out the starfish entirely.

scenes.label: Outbreaks still bad
scenes.say: Now, to be clear, she also says outbreaks are still a real danger. Huge numbers of starfish can still wreck a reef.

scenes.label: It's the numbers
scenes.say: So the starfish isn't the villain. Too many starfish is the villain. A few of them? They might be part of a healthy reef.
So, did you change your answer? Villain or hero? Tell me in the comments. And which secret surprised you the most?

short.title: This Starfish Eats Coral With Its Stomach Outside
short.description: The crown-of-thorns starfish eats coral reefs with its stomach pushed outside its body. But a 2026 Great Barrier Reef study found most of the corals it bites survive, and a few starfish may help reefs stay diverse. Full story on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: This starfish actually eats coral with its stomach outside its body. And scientists just found it might help reefs.

scenes.label: Digests coral outside
scenes.say: It spreads its stomach over living coral like a blanket and digests it. One adult eats up to ten square meters a year.

scenes.label: Up to 90% coral lost
scenes.say: When huge numbers show up at once, these outbreaks can kill up to ninety percent of the coral on a reef.

scenes.label: ~75% survived
scenes.say: But on a calm, protected reef, scientists found the coral survived after almost seventy-five percent of the starfish's meals.

scenes.label: Trims the fast ones
scenes.say: It mostly trims the fast-growing corals that hog the reef, which leaves room for slower kinds to survive. So too many is the problem.

scenes.label: Villain or helper?
scenes.say: A few are fine. So remember, this starfish actually eats coral with its stomach outside its body.
